column5: prepare YHWH's way in wilderness
column6: The commentary treats guidance as showing a real road and making a journey possible. Isaiah's command to prepare YHWH's way and make a highway straight supplies the route-formula that precedes its leveling in 40:4.

column5: prepare the Lord's way
column6: Luke quotes the call to prepare the Lord's way and make his paths straight. It is the Christian continuation that supplies the guide-and-road formula distinct from the terrain changes in Luke 3:5.

column5: remove obstacles from my people's way
column6: A voice orders a way built up and every obstruction removed from the people's path. This directly realizes the commentary's promise of a road made easy for its walker.

column5: build highway and clear stones
column6: The prophet tells people to pass through the gates, build up the highway, and clear its stones. Its public roadwork makes concrete the commentary's eased route rather than a merely inward disposition.

column5: straight path without stumbling
column6: God leads the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble. This closely combines the commentary's guide, light movement, and secure arrival.

column5: people led like a flock
column6: God leads his people out like sheep and guides them through the wilderness like a flock. It gives the commentary's guide-before-followers image an explicitly animal-shaped biblical form.

column5: word as lamp for feet and path
column6: The commentary makes divine guidance a journey and its rejected message a reminder. Psalm 119 calls God's word a lamp for feet and light for a path, joining revelation and locomotion.

column5: commandment as lamp and reproof as way of life
column6: Proverbs calls commandment a lamp, teaching light, and corrective reproofs the way of life. This makes the commentary's admonition something that should direct a traveler rather than be passed by.

column5: God teaches and leads the profitable way
column6: YHWH teaches what benefits and leads Israel in the way it should go. It directly pairs the commentary's divine huda with yusr as a beneficial course.

column5: good Spirit on level ground
column6: The psalm asks that God's good Spirit lead the speaker on level ground. It unites the commentary's leading guide with its balanced, easier terrain.

column5: continual guidance and strengthened bones
column6: YHWH promises continual guidance, satisfaction in dry places, and strength for the bones. Its linked guidance and bodily renewal answer the commentary's weak traveler and easy course.

column5: green pastures and leading beside waters
column6: The commentary moves from pasture to guided travel. Psalm 23 makes the shepherd cause rest in green pastures and lead beside quiet waters, preserving both landscape and direction.

column5: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
column6: The commentary's secondary h-d-y image is a weakened person needing support. Isaiah commands the strengthening of weak hands and unsteady knees before its highway vision.

column5: lame person leaping like a deer
column6: Isaiah's lame person leaps like a deer. This is a sharply specific transformation of weak legs into the light, high-country movement developed in the commentary.

column5: weak hands and feeble knees restored
column6: Hebrews calls for drooping hands and weak knees to be strengthened. Together with its next verse on straight paths, it supplies the bodily side of the commentary's supported traveler.

column5: deer feet and high places
column6: God makes the singer's feet like a deer's and sets him on high places. This repeated biblical formulation independently confirms the commentary's light legs and elevated route.

column5: sweat of the face after exile
column6: The commentary relates Adam's leaving the garden to hardship. Genesis specifies that he will eat bread by the sweat of his face until returning to the ground, intensifying the toil already named in 3:17.

column5: heavy yoke on Adam's children
column6: Sirach describes great toil and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam. It is a Jewish wisdom expansion of the commentary's Adamic movement from garden ease into hardship.

column5: Moses turns aside to see the sign
column6: The commentary treats turning aside from the reminder as the wretched movement. Moses says he will turn aside to see the burning bush, making the same spatial gesture an attentive response to a divine sign.

column5: God calls when Moses has turned aside
column6: When YHWH sees Moses turn aside to look, God calls him by name. This completes the counter-image: a sideways movement that receives, rather than avoids, divine address.

column5: fleeing from YHWH's presence
column6: Jonah physically sets out for Tarshish to flee from YHWH after receiving a commission. The narrative gives the commentary's avoidance of a divine reminder a full journey-shaped enactment.

column5: disciples withdraw and stop walking with Jesus
column6: After Jesus' difficult teaching, many disciples go back and no longer walk with him. It provides a Christian scene of abandoning a guide after hearing his words, close to the commentary's wretched avoidance.

column5: limping between YHWH and Baal
column6: Elijah asks how long Israel will limp between two positions and demands following either YHWH or Baal. It fuses the commentary's uneven walking, forked road, and Abrahamic anti-idolatry concern.

column5: put away foreign gods and purify
column6: Jacob orders his household to put away foreign gods, purify themselves, and change garments. This is a concrete household enactment of the commentary's wish to be kept apart from idols.

column5: turn from futile things to the living Creator
column6: Paul and Barnabas urge idolizing crowds to turn from vain things to the living God who made heaven and earth. It directly connects the commentary's creation claim to its movement away from idolatry.

column5: temple of God versus idols
column6: Paul contrasts the temple of the living God with idols. This establishes the Christian side of the commentary's Abrahamic separation between divine worship and false objects.

column5: come out and be separate
column6: The command to come out from their midst and be separate gives bodily force to the commentary's janb image of keeping oneself away from a thing; its immediate setting is the idol contrast of 6:16.

column5: way of life and way of death
column6: YHWH sets before Jerusalem the way of life and the way of death. The formula supplies a direct prophetic counterpart to the commentary's one journey resolving into opposed ends.

column5: one is led on the path one chooses
column6: The Talmud states that a person is led on the way the person wishes to go. This rabbinic maxim is especially close to the commentary's claim that the same divine easing works toward ease or hardship according to the traveler's direction.

column5: arrogant and evildoers as stubble in fire
column6: In Hebrew WLC versification, the coming day burns the arrogant and evildoers like stubble. It joins the commentary's vegetal residue, wretchedness, and final fire in one prophetic image.

column5: all flesh as withering grass
column6: First Peter repeats that all flesh is grass and that grass withers. It gives the commentary's pasture-to-waste image a Christian scriptural reception centered on mortality.

column5: weary and burdened people invited to rest
column6: Before calling his yoke easy, Jesus invites those laboring and heavily burdened to come for rest. This names the human hardship to which the commentary's promise of ease responds.

column5: commandments not burdensome
column6: First John says love of God keeps his commandments and that those commandments are not burdensome. It provides a concise Christian analogue to the commentary's ease as obedient responsiveness.

column5: Jesus as the way
column6: Jesus identifies himself as the way leading to the Father. This is a concentrated Christian transformation of the commentary's guide, path, and destination pattern.

column5: Jesus walking ahead toward Jerusalem
column6: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus goes ahead of the disciples while they follow in awe and fear. The scene realizes the commentary's guide who moves in front of those on the journey.

column5: following the light without walking in darkness
column6: Jesus says that whoever follows him will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. It makes following the true guide the opposite of the commentary's lost or warning-avoiding traveler.

column5: way to the tree of life guarded after Eden
column6: After expelling Adam, God stations guardians to keep the way to the tree of life. It supplies a route closed by the Edenic fall, a spatial counterpart to the commentary's loss of ease after leaving the garden.

column5: riding on the heights of earth
column6: God promises to make the faithful ride on the heights of the earth. It gives a second prophetic use of riding and high terrain alongside the commentary's mount and mountain ridge.

column5: lead on a level path
column6: The psalm asks to be taught YHWH's way and led on a level path because of enemies. It adds a prayerful use of the commentary's guided, balanced road.

column5: upward path of life away from Sheol
column6: For the prudent, the path of life leads upward in order to turn from Sheol below. It aligns the commentary's elevated road with its contrasting endpoint in the fire, though it does not share the animal imagery.

column5: unfruitful ground ending in burning
column6: Land bearing thorns and thistles is rejected, near a curse, and ends in burning. This extends the commentary's vegetation-and-fire sequence through a Christian agricultural warning.

column5: straying sheep returned to shepherd
column6: People once strayed like sheep but have returned to the shepherd and overseer of their souls. It gives a Christian recovery-from-wrong-route counterpart to the commentary's guide and its animal family.

column5: Creator forms and establishes the earth
column6: The Creator forms, makes, and establishes the earth for habitation rather than emptiness. This enriches the commentary's brief claim that God creates and proportions, though it does not develop the travel imagery.

column5: created for works prepared to walk in
column6: Believers are called God's workmanship, created for works God prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them. It combines the commentary's creation language with a divinely prepared course of action.

column5: God gives the horse its strength
column6: God asks Job whether he gives the horse its strength and clothes its neck. It places the equine capacity behind the commentary's readily led horse within the Creator's ordering of creatures.

column5: garments laid on a mount for Jesus to sit
column6: The commentary develops a cover placed on a camel's hump and a rider settling on the animal. Matthew narrates garments laid on the donkey and colt before Jesus sits, a literal Christian journey image of mount and seat-covering.
